lesson.menu_desc: The discovery call: six questions, no deck, and the silence after each one -- 33 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 5 -- Ask Before You Pitch
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Flávio Masaharu Kuroda | Lesson 5 -- Ask Before You Pitch

listenings.text: I do not demo on a first call. I do not even open the file, and I have stopped apologising for it. The moment a deck is on the screen, the customer stops describing their own problem and starts reacting to my product, and I have never once got the original description back. What I am listening for is two things, and only two. A number and a workaround. A number gives the problem a size: nine days instead of four, eleven steps instead of six, four people instead of one. And a workaround tells me the problem has been there long enough for somebody to build a habit around it, which means somebody has been quietly paying for it every month for years. The last thing, and this is the one that took me longest to learn: after you ask a question, say nothing. The silence is where the useful half of the answer lives. Filling it is the most expensive habit in this job.

I take a lot of these calls, and there is one question almost nobody asks me. Nobody asks what happens today when the process fails. They ask what I want to buy, they ask what my priorities are for next year, they ask about budget in the first ten minutes, and then they tell me about their platform. The ones I remember asked me to walk them through the last time it went wrong. When somebody arrives with the solution already prepared, I can hear it in the first three minutes, because they are selling to a company they invented on the way to the meeting, and it is never quite mine. And here is the part that would surprise them. Some of our worst problems have been there for years and have never been escalated, because escalating something means admitting that it has been normal for a long time. So it stays, everybody works around it, and no vendor ever hears about it, because no vendor ever asks.
